source: Nisbett, Peng, Choi & Norenzayan (2001) Culture and systems of thought: holistic vs analytic cognition (preprint)
finding: Core theory. Ecology and social structure shape habits of attention. East Asians (interdependent, complex fields) attend to the field and relations and use holistic reasoning. Westerners (independent, object-focused) attend to focal objects, assign categories and apply rules. Predicts differences in categorisation, causal attribution, logic, and tolerance of contradiction.
numbers: Theory-level. The paper says many effects are large: ratios of 2 or 3 to 1, and effect sizes often well above 1.00.
quote: If Easterners attribute causality primarily to the field, then it is relationships between the object and the field that might serve as the basis of organization.
limits: Origin story (Greek vs Chinese society) is speculative. Most data are student samples compared across two or three countries.
agent_relevance: Background only. Frames rule-and-category vs relation-and-context as two default organising styles. No direct operator for our schema.

source: Nisbett, Peng, Choi & Norenzayan (2001) Culture and systems of thought: holistic vs analytic cognition (preprint)
finding: Chiu (1972), as reported in the 2001 review: children saw triads of pictures (human, vehicle, furniture, tool, food) and chose two that go together and said why. Chinese children chose relational-contextual pairs; American children chose by category or shared feature.
numbers: Example: man, woman, child. Chinese group woman and child ('the mother takes care of the baby'). Americans group man and woman ('both are adults'). Exact proportions not given in the review.
quote: chose any two of the three objects in a set which were alike or went together and to state the reason
limits: Read through the 2001 review, not the 1972 paper. Children only; no counts in the review.
agent_relevance: This is the triad task that later LLM studies reuse (a21, a23). It tests relational vs taxonomic pairing.

source: Nisbett & Masuda (2007) Culture and point of view, Intellectica
finding: Chiu triad example restated: American children paired chicken and cow ('both are animals'); Chinese children paired cow and grass ('the cow eats the grass'). Same tendency found in college students given word triplets by Ji and Nisbett.
numbers: No counts given in this chapter.
limits: Review-level retelling.
agent_relevance: Concrete picture of the paradigm: three items, pick two, give a reason. The reason matters as much as the pick.

source: Nisbett, Peng, Choi & Norenzayan (2001) Culture and systems of thought: holistic vs analytic cognition (preprint)
finding: Ji and Nisbett (2000), as reported: adult Chinese and American students, tested in their own languages, picked which two of three verbal items were most related. Each triad had a relation pair (pencil, notebook; sky, sunshine) and a category pair (notebook, magazine; sunshine, brightness). Chinese chose relations more; Americans chose categories more. Justifications matched: Chinese 'the sun is in the sky', Americans 'both are in the heavens'.
numbers: Percentages are not in the review.
limits: Read through the review. Ji, Zhang and Nisbett (2004), the language control, could not be opened (all copies blocked).
agent_relevance: Shows a test that separates same-kind from goes-with. Our schema has no such split; analogy vs taxonomy retrieval could use it.

source: Nisbett, Peng, Choi & Norenzayan (2001) Culture and systems of thought: holistic vs analytic cognition (preprint)
finding: Norenzayan, Smith, Kim and Nisbett (2002), as reported: a target object sits under two groups of four. One group looks similar overall (family resemblance). The other group shares one deterministic rule (curved stem). A majority of East Asians matched by family resemblance; a majority of European Americans matched by the rule. Asian Americans split evenly.
numbers: Majority vs majority; exact percentages only in a figure not available as text. Asian Americans about 50/50.
limits: Figure values not read. Kemler-Nelson (1984) paradigm. Tests preference, not ability.
agent_relevance: Classic rule vs similarity conflict. LLMs face this when a surface-similar example disagrees with a stated rule.

source: Nisbett, Peng, Choi & Norenzayan (2001) Culture and systems of thought: holistic vs analytic cognition (preprint)
finding: Category learning (Allen and Brooks paradigm), as reported by the 2001 review: cartoon animals from Venus or Saturn. Exemplar condition: guess with feedback. Rule condition: any 3 of 5 features means Venus. East Asians and Americans did equally well in the exemplar condition. In the rule condition East Asians were slower, and made more errors when rule and similarity conflicted.
numbers: No extra errors when rule and similarity agreed. Asian Americans matched European Americans in speed and accuracy. Counts not in review.
limits: Group sizes not given in the review. Effect is about rule use under conflict, not about overall learning.
agent_relevance: A clean test of following the stated rule even when an example looks different. Fits our G3 style held-out checks.

source: Nisbett, Peng, Choi & Norenzayan (2001) Culture and systems of thought: holistic vs analytic cognition (preprint)
finding: Choi, Nisbett and Smith (1997), as reported: in category-based induction, Koreans were less affected than Americans by premise coverage of the category. Naming the category in the conclusion ('mammals') did nothing for Americans but raised Koreans' use of the category.
numbers: No numbers in review.
limits: Read through the review only.
agent_relevance: Category use depends on salience cues. For an LLM, naming the category in the prompt may switch its taxonomic mode on.

source: Nisbett, Peng, Choi & Norenzayan (2001) Culture and systems of thought: holistic vs analytic cognition (preprint)
finding: Norenzayan, Choi and Nisbett (2000), as reported: Koreans showed a large typicality effect in judging argument convincingness; European Americans did not; Asian Americans in between. Making typicality salient made all groups show it equally. In syllogisms, Koreans showed more belief bias on valid arguments with implausible conclusions, with equal performance on abstract items.
numbers: Group sizes and means not in the review.
quote: this difference cannot be attributed to cultural differences in the ability to reason logically
limits: Preference, not ability, shown by equal abstract-item performance and by the salience manipulation.
agent_relevance: Belief bias vs logic is a known LLM failure. The cultural finding says the same split can be a default, not a capacity.

source: Nisbett, Peng, Choi & Norenzayan (2001) Culture and systems of thought: holistic vs analytic cognition (preprint)
finding: Masuda and Nisbett (2001), as reported: animated underwater scenes shown to Japanese and Americans, then free recall. Americans began with the focal fish; Japanese began with the background. Equal statements about the focal fish; Japanese made about 70 percent more background statements and about 100 percent more statements on relations with inanimate things. Recognition: Japanese were hurt by a wrong background; Americans were not.
numbers: About 70 percent more background statements; about 100 percent more relation statements. N not given in this review.
limits: Read through the review; the 2006 paper says more than 60 percent and the PNAS review says 65 percent, so the figure varies by telling.
agent_relevance: Binding of object to context in memory. An agent that ignores context gets focal items right but misses context changes.

source: Norenzayan, Choi & Peng, Cultural psychology handbook chapter (cognition and culture)
finding: Handbook chapter restates Masuda and Nisbett (2001): scenes had focal fish (larger, brighter, faster) among rocks, plants, and small fish. Japanese began with context. Equal statements on the focal fish. About 70 percent more statements on the field. Twice as many on relations with inert background objects.
numbers: 70 percent; 2x.
limits: Chapter, not the original JPSP paper (could not open).
agent_relevance: Second source agrees on the main figures of a09.

source: Nisbett & Masuda (2003) Culture and point of view, PNAS 100
finding: PNAS review restates Masuda and Nisbett (2001): Americans mentioned salient objects first far more often; Japanese mentioned the field almost twice as often and made 65 percent more field observations. Japanese made more errors with a novel background; Americans did not.
numbers: 65 percent more field observations; first mentions about 2x on field.
limits: Review. Take the effect as roughly 60 to 70 percent more background statements.
agent_relevance: Numbers differ across tellings of the same study. Our agent should store the source of each number.

source: Masuda & Nisbett (2006) Culture and change blindness, Cognitive Science 30
finding: Change blindness, Experiment 1 (flicker paradigm, 30 pairs of still photos, up to 60 s). East Asians found context changes faster than Americans. Americans found focal-object changes faster than context changes; East Asians found both equally fast.
numbers: 30 Americans and 36 East Asian international students at Michigan. Culture x change type F(1,64)=3.96, p=.05. East Asians faster on context F(1,64)=4.02, p<.05. Americans faster on object than context F(1,64)=5.45, p<.03.
limits: Weak interaction (p=.05). East Asians were international students in the US. No effect size given.
agent_relevance: Shows the focal advantage is a default of one group, not a general law of perception.

source: Masuda & Nisbett (2006) Culture and change blindness, Cognitive Science 30
finding: Experiment 2: animated vignettes, five scenes, changes to focal object or context. Japanese found more context changes. Americans were marginally better on object changes.
numbers: 19 Americans (Michigan) and 18 Japanese (Kyoto). Interaction F(1,35)=9.44, p<.005. Context: Japanese more, F(1,35)=5.68, p<.03. Object: Americans marginally more, F(1,35)=2.92, .05<p<.10. 5.4 percent of answers were incorrect and dropped.
limits: Small groups. Scenes were mostly American in origin, which may favour the American pattern.
agent_relevance: Small sample; treat as a direction, not a size.

source: Masuda & Nisbett (2006) Culture and change blindness, Cognitive Science 30
finding: Experiment 3: replication with Japanese-looking scenes added (more objects, more complex). Interaction replicated with much stronger statistics. Both cultures found object changes more often in American scenes and context changes more often in Japanese scenes. No culture x scene-type interaction.
numbers: 28 Americans and 32 Japanese. Culture x attention F(1,58)=22.72, p<.001. Context: Japanese more F(1,58)=16.17, p<.001. Object: Americans more F(1,58)=5.63, p<.02. Attention x scene type F(1,58)=128.62, p<.001. Culturally neutral scenes: object-change difference slight and not significant.
limits: Object-change difference vanished in neutral scenes, so the effect rests mostly on context attention. Environment effect is as large as the culture effect.
agent_relevance: The scene itself steers attention. For an agent, input format (cluttered vs clean) may matter more than a persona.

source: Masuda & Nisbett (2006) Culture and change blindness, Cognitive Science 30
finding: Environment as a cause. Miyamoto, Nisbett and Masuda photographed 1,000 scenes near schools, hotels and post offices in US and Japanese towns of three sizes. Japanese scenes had more objects and more complexity. Priming with Japanese scenes made both Americans and Japanese detect more context changes.
numbers: 1,000 scenes; Japanese scenes averaged 32 percent more objects (per the 2003 review). The authors say environment is not the whole story.
limits: Reported second-hand inside the 2006 paper. Effect size of priming not given here.
agent_relevance: Attention style can be primed. This links to the sister subfield on priming of orientation.

source: Chua, Boland & Nisbett (2005) Cultural variation in eye movements during scene perception, PNAS
finding: Eye tracking. Americans fixated the focal object sooner and longer. Chinese made more background fixations and showed no object preference until later. Chinese were less accurate when objects appeared on new backgrounds.
numbers: 21 Americans and 24 Chinese analysed (of 25 and 27 recruited); 36 pictures, 3 s each, 120 Hz tracker. Americans first fixated the object 118 ms sooner, t(43)=2.41, p=.02. Chinese more fixations F(1,43)=4.43, all from background F(1,43)=9.50. Culture x region interaction from about 420 ms F(1,43)=6.43. 420 to 1,100 ms Americans favoured objects F(1,43)=7.31. 1,100 to 3,000 ms Chinese favoured backgrounds F(1,43)=6.64. Recognition on new backgrounds F(1,44)=5.72, p=.02.
limits: Only 2 of 18 correlations between eye data and memory were marginal. Gaps between groups are in timing, not in total looks.
agent_relevance: Key target of the failed replications, see a17.

source: Rayner, Li, Williams, Cave & Well (2007); Rayner, Castelhano & Yang (2009); Evans et al. (2009): eye-movement non-replications (search-result summary only)
finding: Per a search summary: Rayner et al. 2007 tested native English and native Chinese speakers on six tasks and found no sign Chinese looked longer at backgrounds. Rayner et al. 2009 found no cultural differences for typical or unusual scenes. Evans et al. 2009 found equal accuracy drop, response bias and eye patterns across cultures.
numbers: No numbers read. Search summary only.
limits: I could not open these (PMC blocked by a verification page). Angle B or C should check them. Boland and colleagues later reported divergence in some measures.
agent_relevance: The strongest challenge to the attention claim at the eye level. Treat eye-level cultural effects as unsettled.

source: Nisbett & Masuda (2003) Culture and point of view, PNAS 100
finding: Other attention studies summarised: Hedden et al. (Chinese, not Americans, recall words better when shown on social backgrounds); Ji et al. covariation (Chinese detected more covariation and were better calibrated); rod and frame (Chinese more influenced by the frame); Chinese predicted trend reversals in all but 1 of 12 curve conditions.
numbers: Chinese predicted reversals in 11 of 12 conditions.
limits: Review page gave no N, F or p.
agent_relevance: Field dependence is one family of results and categorisation is another. The theory ties them to one attention style.

source: Nisbett & Masuda (2007) Culture and point of view, Intellectica
finding: Review for a French audience. Repeats Chiu triads, family resemblance, rule vs similarity, field attention. Notes that the language of testing for bilinguals is generally not predictive of results (Norenzayan et al. 2002).
limits: Review; no new data.
agent_relevance: Language of testing is a weak lever in humans, so LLM prompt-language results (a22, a23) are not clearly the same effect.

source: Nisbett, Peng, Choi & Norenzayan (2001) Culture and systems of thought: holistic vs analytic cognition (preprint)
finding: Ji and Nisbett found that English-speaking Chinese used relationships more and categories less when they grouped words in Chinese than in English. The authors treat social practice and cognition as in mutual equilibrium.
limits: Mixed message: language shifts the pattern in this study but the 2007 chapter says language is generally not predictive.
agent_relevance: Prompt language may shift a model as it can shift bilinguals; but see a22.

source: Jin et al. (2023) The Cultural Psychology of LLMs: Is ChatGPT a holistic or analytic thinker?
finding: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 leaned holistic on the Analysis-Holism Scale and on a 20-item triadic categorisation task. Value scales (dialectical self, self-construal) did not clearly lean East or West.
numbers: 10 runs per model at temperature 1. AHS: GPT-3.5 5.35 (SD 0.11), GPT-4 5.01 (SD 0.10) vs human norm 4.87 (SD 0.49, N=702). Triad relational share GPT-3.5 0.87 (SD 0.06), GPT-4 0.85 (SD 0.05); above the mean of most Chinese provinces. Held across temperature 0 to 1.5 and prompt language.
limits: Only 10 runs and 20 items (10 real). Self-report scales applied to a model. The authors suggest training method or data as cause.
agent_relevance: Frontier LLMs pair by relation on triads far more than humans do. A text agent already sits at the relational end; no push toward rules is built in.

source: Sun & Wang (2025) The fragility of cultural tendencies in LLMs
finding: Re-test of Lu, Song and Zhang, who said GPT and ERNIE are more holistic and interdependent in Chinese than in English. With 8 models, 30 to 60 items per task, temperature 0, prompt language had little effect.
numbers: 8 models: gpt-4.1, gemini-2.5, claude-sonnet-4, grok-4, kimi-k2, deepseek-V3, ernie-4.5, qwen3-30b. 4 tasks plus 1 picture task. No overall language or origin effect (p=.15, .25, 1.0, .917). Only a few models moved: deepseek and qwen preferred Chinese (0.01<p<0.05).
limits: Items were adapted, not exact, because the originals were not released. Tasks are attribution, change belief, syllogism, interpersonal expectation; no triad categorisation.
agent_relevance: Do not expect persona or prompt language to reliably switch an LLM between analytic and holistic. Do not build a mode switch on it.

source: Hu et al. (2026) Machine culture: 2x2 US vs China model by English vs Chinese prompt, eight tasks (Task 4 triads)
finding: Task 4 is a triad categorisation (seagull, sky, dog). Language did not shift relational vs categorical pairing. The US model paired by relation more than the Chinese model, the opposite of the human pattern.
numbers: US model R-C score M=8.10 (SD 1.44) vs Chinese model 6.04 (SD 1.54), t=-13.81, p<.001, d=1.38, CI [-2.34,-1.78]. Language: Chinese prompt 7.10 (SD 2.15) vs English 7.04 (SD 1.40), t(342.66)=0.33, p=.741, d=0.03. About 400 observations per task.
limits: Two models only (GPT-4o and a Chinese model). Seed and prompt effects not isolated.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM test of the Chiu triad. Model origin and prompt language did not predict the human pattern.

source: Hu et al. (2026) Machine culture: Task 1 scene generation and Task 2 scene description
finding: Attention tasks. Chinese prompts produced more objects in generated landscapes (holistic direction) but no higher horizon. In scene description, English prompts gave more objects than Chinese (opposite of the holistic prediction).
numbers: Generated objects: Chinese M=10.71 (SD 4.70) vs English 8.91 (SD 2.26), t(286.19)=4.88, d=0.49. Horizon 523.20 vs 530.06, p=.096. Description objects: English 10.90 vs Chinese 10.06, t(374.94)=-3.60, d=0.36.
limits: The authors suggest verbose English output reflects data density, not holistic attention.
agent_relevance: Counting objects is a poor stand-in for attention style. Use a behavioural probe, such as change detection with a planted change in context.

source: Sabir et al. (2025) Contrasting cognitive styles in vision-language models: holistic attention in Japanese vs analytical focus in English
finding: VLM captions on COCO (Western) and Japanese-image datasets were classed holistic or analytic. Captions written in Japanese were more holistic. Japanese-content images raised the holistic share. Model size mattered.
numbers: GPT-4o-JP 6-shot: 26.10 percent holistic on COCO vs 73.37 percent on the 1K Japanese dataset. 1K random COCO, 6-shot: GPT-4o 26.2, Gemma-3-27B 19.2, Gemma-3-27B-JP 28.8, GPT4o-JP 35.5 percent. Translating captions shifted the holistic ratio by an average of 13.21 percent.
limits: Holistic or analytic is labelled by a model (checked on 200 human-rated images). Uses description order, not categorisation.
agent_relevance: Image content can change style as much as language; same lesson as the scene-environment finding in humans (a15).

source: Synthesis across a01 to a25 (my own summary, not a source claim)
finding: Human categorisation differences rest on small studies of East Asian vs American students. Eye-level support is mixed (a16, a17). LLM tests show frontier models near the relational end on triads, with weak and unstable prompt-language effects (a21 to a23).
numbers: Human N per study: 18 to 36 per group in the Masuda papers, 45 in Chua. LLM runs: 10 per model (Jin), about 400 observations per task (Hu).
limits: This line is synthesis.
agent_relevance: Keep as background. Do not add an operator from this subfield (section 4b).

source: Chua, Boland & Nisbett (2005) Cultural variation in eye movements during scene perception, PNAS
finding: Measures that do not fit a simple story. Both groups fixated backgrounds more than objects overall. Chinese gave higher liking ratings. The attention shift is relative, not absolute.
numbers: Overall background > object F(1,43)=72.46. Longer fixations on objects than backgrounds in both groups F(1,43)=17.27; larger for Americans F(1,43)=5.97, p<.02. Liking 4.64 vs 4.16, p<.005. About 32 to 35 percent of both groups already looked at the object at picture onset.
limits: Raw means are only in figures. The abstract says saccades to the background but the results report fixations.
agent_relevance: Effect is a matter of degree and timing. Treat holistic vs analytic as a gradient, not a binary.

source: Hu et al. (2026) vs Jin et al. (2023): triad results compared
finding: Two LLM triad results disagree on how to read the model. Jin reports a high relational share for GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 (0.85 to 0.87) and calls it holistic. Hu finds the US model more relational than the Chinese model and no language effect.
numbers: Jin: 0.85 to 0.87 relational, 20 items. Hu: R-C 8.10 vs 6.04, d=1.38.
limits: Different scoring and item sets; not directly comparable.
agent_relevance: Results depend on the item set. Test with your own triads.
